lesson.title: Spotting the Pattern: When an Integral Becomes a Natural Log
lesson.summary: Whenever an integrand's numerator matches the derivative of its denominator, the integral collapses to a natural log, a pattern that generalizes the base rule for 1/x.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter established the base case: integral of (1/x) dx = ln|x| + C. This chapter generalizes that idea to a much wider class of integrals that all reduce to a natural log in the end.

The general pattern is this: for a differentiable function f(x), integral of f'(x)/f(x) dx = ln|f(x)| + C, wherever f(x) is not equal to 0. The reasoning is the chain rule applied to the derivative of ln|x|, and then run backward. Differentiating ln|f(x)| with the chain rule gives (1/f(x)) * f'(x), which is the same thing as f'(x)/f(x). Since that derivative computation produces exactly f'(x)/f(x), reading it backward tells you that ln|f(x)| is an antiderivative of f'(x)/f(x). Notice that integral of (1/x) dx = ln|x| + C is just the special case of this pattern where f(x) = x, since the derivative of x is 1.

This explains why the natural logarithm keeps reappearing throughout integral calculus. Any time you are integrating a fraction and you notice that the top is, or can be rewritten as, a constant multiple of the derivative of the bottom, the answer is a natural log of the bottom, no more complicated technique needed.

Worked example: find integral of x/(x^2+4) dx. The derivative of the denominator x^2+4 is 2x, and the numerator is x, which is exactly half of 2x. Rewrite the integrand to expose that relationship: x/(x^2+4) = (1/2) * [2x/(x^2+4)]. Now pull the constant 1/2 outside using the constant multiple rule: (1/2) * integral of [2x/(x^2+4)] dx = (1/2) * ln|x^2+4| + C. Since x^2+4 is always positive, the absolute value bars can be dropped, giving (1/2)*ln(x^2+4) + C. Verify by differentiating: the derivative of (1/2)*ln(x^2+4) is (1/2) * (2x)/(x^2+4), and the 2's cancel, leaving x/(x^2+4), which matches the original integrand exactly.

The same pattern handles other fractions built from familiar functions. For instance, since tan(x) can be written as sin(x)/cos(x), and the derivative of cos(x) is -sin(x), rewriting tan(x) as -(-sin(x))/cos(x) exposes the numerator as the derivative of the denominator, up to a sign, giving integral of tan(x) dx = -ln|cos(x)| + C. Recognizing this numerator-matches-derivative-of-denominator shape, rather than trying to memorize each case separately, is the real skill this chapter is building.
